query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Premelting in iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is controlled by the surface segregation of copper due to its lower melting point, a behavior that can be mitigated by increasing the relative nickel content, which facilitates copper dissolution into a homogeneous liquid phase.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, equiatomic iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper nanoparticles with uniform microstructure and compositional homogeneity.
generation.intervention: Synthesize two batches of HEA nanoparticles: one with the baseline equiatomic composition and a second with an increased Ni/Cu ratio (e.g., raise Ni from 20 at% to ~25 at% and reduce Cu from 20 at% to ~15 at% while keeping Fe, Cr, and Co constant).
generation.conditions: Perform controlled heating experiments in an inert (vacuum or high-purity argon) atmosphere using in situ neutron imaging and complementary DSC across the premelting and melting temperature range (approximately 1000 °C to 1500 °C), with discrete temperature increments (e.g., every 20 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution (or suppression) of a Cu-rich surface phase on nanoparticles, which mediates the onset of premelting and subsequent melting behavior.
generation.mechanism: Due to its inherently lower melting point, copper tends to segregate to the particle surface upon heating, initiating premelting. Addition of extra nickel increases the solubility of copper within the alloy melt, reducing the extent of copper segregation through improved atomic mixing. This leads to a delayed, more homogeneous transition from solid to liquid, with a higher onset of premelting and melting temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with increased Ni/Cu ratio will exhibit a delayed onset of Cu surface segregation and a measurable increase in the premelting and melting temperatures (on the order of 15–30 °C higher) compared to the baseline equiatomic nanoparticles.
generation.baseline: Baseline equiatomic iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper nanoparticles are expected to show early onset of premelting indicated by the formation of a Cu-rich surface phase around ~1100 °C and complete melting near ~1420 °C, as inferred from analogous systems.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to HEA nanoparticles in the size range where surface and grain-boundary diffusion are pronounced (typically 10–100 nm) and under conditions of controlled inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation.
generation.uncertainty: Exact shifts in premelting and melting temperatures may depend on particle size distribution, synthesis conditions, and annealing history. Variations in local diffusivity and unintentional contamination could also affect the observed behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct side-by-side in situ neutron imaging and DSC measurements on baseline equiatomic nanoparticles and Ni-enhanced nanoparticles while ramping the temperature under identical inert atmosphere conditions. Utilize EDX mapping to monitor copper distribution on the particle surfaces as a function of temperature.
measurements: Onset temperature at which Cu-rich regions emerge (via imaging and EDX)
Quantitative elemental maps of nanoparticles at selected temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-enhanced nanoparticles do not exhibit a statistically significant delay (e.g., less than ~15 °C difference) in the appearance of Cu-rich surface segregation or in the premelting/melting transitions compared to the baseline, or if copper segregation occurs similarly in both samples, the hypothesis that increased nickel content modulates premelting by suppressing copper segregation is falsified.

The CoCrCuNi alloy has been previously shown to solidify into a uniform dendritic microstructure from arc-melting [], which is indicative that the microstructure evolved from a single-phase liquid as opposed to the large-scale macroscopic-phase separation that has been observed in similar alloys of CoCrCu [] and CoCrCuFe []. However, there are no reported slow cooling solidification studies on the CoCrCuNi alloy. Previous neutron imaging of the CoCrCu by the present authors resulted in neutron radiographs of the CoCrCu displaying the buttons melting and separating based on density []. The stacking of the liquid immiscible phases of CoCr-rich liquid and Cu-rich liquid was characterized by their differences in neutron attenuation. The same experiment was essentially repeated for this work with the equiatomic addition of Ni buttons such that the equiatomic CoCrCu becomes equiatomic CoCrCuNi once melting and dissolution has occurred. This allows for a more equilibrium solidification due to the slow cooling, as well as an opportunity to image the remixing of the immiscible CoCr-rich and Cu-rich liquid phases.

papers.title: In-Situ Imaging of Molten High-Entropy Alloys Using Cold Neutrons.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoCrCu and CoCrCuNi high-entropy alloys (button samples)
papers.approach: In situ neutron imaging during controlled heating and cooling cycles; added Ni buttons to the CoCrCu system to observe alloying behavior during melting and solidification.
papers.findings: The radiographs show the onset of melting at ~1100 °C, complete dissolution (miscibility) at ~1420 °C, and subsequent solidification. In the CoCrCu system, a Cu‐rich phase emerges on the surface, but the addition of Ni facilitates the remixing of phase‐separated liquids into a single, uniform phase.
papers.mechanism: Ni acts as a solubility pathway for Cu, thereby enabling transition from an initially phase‐separated (immiscible) system to a homogenous single-phase liquid, which then solidifies uniformly.

papers.title: Atomic Simulations of Grain Structures and Deformation Behaviors in Nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations were used to study the melting properties of HEAs as a function of grain size, alongside deformation analyses under strain.
papers.findings: The simulations predict that the melting temperature strongly decreases with decreasing grain size (e.g., from ~1940 K for a perfect FCC crystal to ~1340 K when grains are reduced to 2.5 nm). At very small sizes, amorphization blurs the sharp volume change seen during melting.
papers.mechanism: Enhanced grain-boundary diffusion and structural disorder (including the onset of amorphization) in nanoparticles modify the thermal response, leading to depressed melting points compared to bulk materials.

papers.title: Evaluation of Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu System and Subsequent Derivation of a Non-Equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu Alloy.
papers.approach: Controlled slow cooling experiments from the liquid state using a furnace with a double crucible, designed to minimize thermal gradients and oxidation.
papers.findings: The experiments reveal that during slow cooling, phase segregation occurs with the formation of Cr-rich crystallites distinct from a nearly equiatomic primary matrix. The kinetic aspects of cooling (e.g., cooling rate, diffusion of different elements) influence the extent of segregation versus formation of a solid solution.
papers.mechanism: Kinetic control during cooling leads to differential alloying; the sequential dissolution of elements during solidification (influenced by their diffusivities and melting points) governs the ultimate microstructure, hinting at a similar kinetic influence on premelting behavior.

established: Nanoparticles exhibit depressed melting temperatures compared to their bulk counterparts due to grain-boundary and size effects.
In situ neutron imaging can capture the detailed evolution of phase changes during melting and solidification in high-entropy alloys.
The chemical complexity inherent to HEAs (e.g., the specific roles of Ni and Cu) significantly affects miscibility and phase transition behavior during thermal cycling.
Molecular dynamics simulations confirm that structural disorder and enhanced diffusion at nanoscale dimensions contribute to reduced melting points and altered premelting phenomena.

approaches_tried.approach: In situ neutron imaging during thermal cycling
approaches_tried.outcome: Direct visualization of melting onset, phase separation (Cu-rich surface in CoCrCu), and the transformation to a homogeneous liquid upon Ni addition.
Prediction of grain size-dependent melting behavior; showed that smaller grains lead to depressed melting temperatures and amorphization effects.
Elucidated the kinetic influences during phase formation and solidification; highlighted how cooling rate and elemental diffusivities affect phase segregation versus solid solution formation.

mechanisms: Ni addition facilitates the homogenization of an otherwise phase-separated CoCrCu system by providing a solubility pathway for Cu, leading to a single-phase liquid during melting.
Enhanced grain-boundary diffusion and amorphization in nanoparticles lower the melting point compared to the bulk, altering the premelting thermal response.

Kinetic control during thermal processing (including the rates of heating and cooling) governs the sequence of elemental dissolution and re-alloying, crucial for both premelting behavior and subsequent solidification.
disagreements: While some studies emphasize the thermodynamic role of elemental miscibility (e.g., the role of Ni in promoting Cu solubility), others suggest that kinetic limitations (such as diffusion rates and cooling rates) are equally determining in phase formation.

There is some debate on the exact influence of particle size and grain boundary effects (i.e., the balance between amorphization and liquid-like behavior) on the observed depression of the melting point, with simulations and experiments sometimes yielding differing insights.
open_questions: Is the onset of premelting in iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper nanoparticles governed primarily by surface segregation phenomena, grain-boundary diffusion, or kinetic alloying effects?

How do specific compositional variations (for example, differences in Ni and Cu ratio) quantitatively alter the melting and premelting transition temperatures in these chemically complex nanoparticles?

What is the interplay between kinetic constraints (e.g., cooling rate, diffusion barriers) and thermodynamic driving forces (miscibility, structural disorder) in dictating the premelting and melting behavior of HEA nanoparticles?
opportunities: Design experiments that combine in situ neutron imaging with controlled compositional variations to directly measure how modifications (e.g., deliberate Ni/Cu ratio changes) affect the onset and progression of melting.
Integrate molecular dynamics simulations specifically tailored for iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper systems to map out the influence of grain size and structural disorder on thermal response.
Implement systematic controlled cooling experiments with variable cooling rates to decouple kinetic effects from equilibrium thermodynamic behavior.

Develop a multifaceted experimental framework that combines real-time thermal analysis (e.g., DSC) with advanced imaging techniques to decisively test the proposed mechanisms governing premelting and melting behavior.

directions.direction: Composition design to modify Ni/Cu ratio and test its effect on copper segregation during heating.
directions.assessment: This approach directly tests the role of elemental miscibility by altering the Ni/Cu balance. Prior studies (e.g., PMC8320920) have shown that Ni facilitates the incorporation of Cu into a homogeneous liquid; therefore, increasing Ni should suppress early Cu surface segregation. The physics of diffusion and melting point differences support this concept, and changing alloy composition is experimentally feasible.

directions.direction: Grain size and microstructure control via synthesis adjustments to evaluate surface and grain-boundary mediated premelting.
directions.assessment: This direction tests whether size-dependent enhanced diffusion and grain-boundary effects govern the onset of premelting. Evidence from MD simulations (PMC6479918) indicates that smaller grains tend to have depressed melting temperatures. This study would be informative but may convolve size effects with compositional effects, complicating interpretation for chemically complex HEA nanoparticles.

directions.direction: Kinetic studies using variable heating and cooling rates to decouple thermodynamic miscibility effects from kinetic diffusion limitations.
directions.assessment: Controlling the heating rate and monitoring the onset of premelting can help decouple steady state thermodynamic effects from kinetic limitations such as diffusion. Although practical and supported by slower cooling studies (PMC10056590), this approach may not directly address the chemical segregation mechanism responsible for premelting.

directions.direction: In situ imaging and real-time spectroscopy during thermal cycling to monitor phase segregation evolution.
directions.assessment: Real-time in situ neutron imaging (PMC8320920) combined with spatially resolved EDX can directly track the appearance of Cu-rich regions during heating. While this approach provides direct visual evidence, it requires complex instrumentation and may be less straightforward to link causally to individual compositional effects.

directions.direction: Molecular dynamics simulations of elemental diffusion and phase change to predict the role of surface segregation on premelting.
directions.assessment: Atomistic simulations can be used to predict how differences in elemental diffusivity (especially of Cu and Ni) drive surface segregation during premelting. This is supported by simulation evidence (PMC6479918), but ultimately experimental validation is necessary. The approach can guide experiments but may be limited by the inherent approximations in simulation interatomic potentials.

choice.direction: Composition design to modify Ni/Cu ratio and test its effect on copper segregation during heating.
choice.why: This direction directly targets the hypothesized mechanism that copper’s lower melting point drives surface segregation during the premelting phase, and that nickel facilitates copper dissolution into the liquid state, homogenizing the melt. It respects all constraints of the system, is supported by prior in situ imaging work (PMC8320920) and MD simulations (PMC6479918), and is feasible and informative through controlled compositional modifications.
